name: PT Bank Pembangunan Daerah Jawa Timur Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Jatim: a regional champion priced as a broken book
frontmatter.summary: Bank Jatim is East Java's regional development bank and the parent of a five-member bank group. The shares trade near half of book value while the parent still earns a double-digit return on equity and pays out more than half of its profit. We think the discount reflects a legacy asset-quality scare and a misread consolidation rather than a permanent loss of earning power. Initiate BUY.
thesis: The group consolidation enlarges the balance sheet but not the parent profit: the five member banks contribute growth and a large minority interest, so this is a capital and franchise story rather than an earnings step-change.

The funding franchise is the moat: cheap provincial deposits and a consumer-led loan book hold the consolidated margin near the mid single digits, even though the parent's own interest income is flat year on year.

Asset quality is the bear case and it is public: a gross non-performing ratio near four percent, heavy write-offs, restructured loans and a state audit finding are all disclosed, yet the shares price a permanent loss of value.
The dividend is the return engine: a payout above half of profit on a yield in the low teens pays the investor to wait for the discount to close.
The catalyst is time and disclosure: a cleaner legacy book and a full year of group reporting give the market an earnings base it can value.

catalysts.event: Year-end position, loan-loss coverage and restructured-loan balances
Full-year results and the board dividend proposal
Annual general meeting and dividend approval
Public expose on group integration and synergy targets

blocks.text: Bank Jatim is the regional development bank of East Java and, after completing its bank-group programme, the parent of five smaller provincial banks. The shares trade at 0.5x of book on a trailing dividend yield of 11.5%, while the parent entity still earned 11.8% on equity in the last financial year [S24]. We initiate coverage with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp679, 48.7% above the last close of Rp492 [S10].

The market is not wrong to be cautious. The bank wrote off more than a trillion rupiah of loans in the last financial year at a recovery rate below a fifth, its gross non-performing loan ratio nearly doubled to 3.9%, and the state auditor documented weak credit analysis across nine branches [S13][S21]. Those are real facts, and they explain why the shares sit where they do.

What the market is doing, in our view, is treating a public asset-quality problem as a permanent capital impairment. The discount is too wide for the earning power that survives it. Three things drive our value. First, the margin: the group earns about 6.6% on earning assets because provincial deposits are cheap, and nine-month consolidated net interest income was IDR7.24tn [S25]. Second, the payout: more than half of profit is distributed, and on today's price that is a yield that compounds while the discount closes [S5][S7]. Third, the book: parent equity stood at IDR13.65tn at the last year end and book value per share is Rp909, so a re-rating towards book value is a large move in the share price [S24].

The main thing we could be wrong about is the durability of the margin in a system where deposit competition is intensifying and credit is growing faster than deposits [S20]. That is the bear case, and it is costed in section five.

Bank Jatim is a regional development bank owned by the provincial government of East Java and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange [S4][S10]. Its franchise is built on the provincial treasury: it holds the cash of the regional government and its agencies, lends to the provincial civil service and to small businesses in the province, and channels development spending into the regional economy [S5][S12]. Management frames the strategy around five pillars — governance and risk management, ecosystem-based business, people, technology and group synergy — and a stated ambition to be the leading regional development bank in the country [S12].

Regional development banks are owned by provincial governments and were created to hold public-sector
deposits and finance regional development. Their funding advantage comes from the treasury float,
which is cheap and sticky, and their lending skews to civil-servant mortgages, payroll lending and
small business credit. That structure produces a higher margin than a commercial bank of similar size,
and a loan book that is sensitive to the provincial budget cycle.

The loan book is consumer-led. At the last year end the parent's own book of IDR67.24tn split into consumer loans of IDR36.54tn, which grew by a twentieth, and a productive book that grew more slowly; management describes the strategy as selective lending into prospective sectors while deepening consumer penetration [S12][S13]. The consolidated book of IDR110.50tn is nearly twice the parent's because five member banks sit inside the group [S12].

The funding side is the heart of the model. Current accounts, the cheapest deposit, reached IDR21.40tn at the last year end and grew by an eighth, while deposit customers rose to 10,915,749 [S12]. Management explicitly describes its strategy as shifting the deposit mix towards cheap funds through transaction banking and ecosystem-based business, and it issued bonds to lengthen the stable-fund base [S12][S5]. That mix produces the margin we model, and it is also what makes the bank sensitive when provincial balances move: group deposits fell between the last year end and the third quarter of the current year as transfers to the regions declined [S17].

The group structure is the fact that most shapes the accounts. Bank Jatim is the parent of a bank group of five provincial banks — Bank NTB Syariah, Bank Banten, Bank Lampung, Bank Sultra and Bank NTT — a structure completed at the end of last year [S12][S3]. It is a regulatory construction under the minimum-core-capital rule rather than a conventional acquisition: the parent supplies capital, liquidity and technology to members whose provincial governments remain significant shareholders, and it consolidates them because it controls them, not because it owns all of their economics [S8][S4]. The ownership split is disclosed: non-controlling interests hold 96.8% of Bank NTB Syariah, 96.6% of Bank Banten and 95.9% of Bank Lampung [S24]. That is why the consolidated balance sheet of IDR168.85tn is far larger than the parent's own book, and why minorities took IDR0.76tn of the IDR1.86tn nine-month consolidated profit [S25].

Operationally the bank runs a conventional branch network across East Java, a sharia unit and a digital franchise. JConnect is the group's digital brand, with mobile and corporate channels, QRIS acceptance and partner-payment services that are being rolled out to member banks; the bank also runs an agent network for outreach beyond its branches [S12][S2]. The bank reports 4,338 employees [S10].

The Indonesian banking system held IDR9,245.00tn of credit at the end of the third quarter, up 13.3% year on year, a rate that has been slowing through the year as the base effect and tighter liquidity bite [S20][S22]. System deposits grew more slowly than credit, at 8.2%, which is the single most important industry fact for a deposit-funded lender: loan growth is running ahead of funding growth, and the deposit market is where the competition is [S20]. By loan type, investment and corporate credit are growing fastest while household and micro credit lag, so the mix is shifting towards the segments where large banks have the advantage [S20].

Bank Jatim is a regional champion rather than a national challenger. It is one of the smaller listed banks by market capitalisation, and it is the parent of a five-member BPD group, the structure the minimum-core-capital rule was designed to produce [S12][S8]. Its market share inside East Java is protected by the provincial treasury relationship and by the payroll and mortgage flows that come with it; outside the province it has little presence, which is precisely why the group structure matters to growth [S3][S5].

The regulatory framework is the industry's main structural driver. The minimum-core-capital rule obliges smaller banks either to raise capital or to join a bank group with a stronger parent, and Bank Jatim has used that rule to become the parent of five provincial banks [S8][S12]. For the parent the benefit is scale, fee and funding synergies and a larger platform; the cost is a large minority interest, consolidation of weaker balance sheets and the integration risk that comes with five different management teams [S3][S4].

Indonesian banking regulation sets a minimum core capital requirement for commercial banks and lets
smaller banks meet it by joining a bank group led by a stronger institution, with the lead bank
supplying capital, liquidity and technology. Provincial development banks are owned by provincial
governments, so the group structure is as much a political arrangement between provinces as a
commercial one. The regulator also supervises the lead bank's responsibility for the group, which
makes integration a supervised obligation rather than an option.

On the five forces, the threat of new entrants is low for the core franchise because the provincial treasury relationship is effectively reserved; rivalry is high and rising in consumer lending and in digital payments; the bargaining power of depositors is rising as the system competes for funds; substitutes in the form of fintech lending and digital wallets are taking share in micro and consumer credit; and the bargaining power of borrowers is limited outside the corporate segment. The net effect is a franchise that is defensible at home and hard to export, which supports the margin and caps the growth rate [S12][S20].

The macro backdrop is mixed for a rate-sensitive lender. The house macro deck carries a cautious regime with balance-of-payments pressure, a rupiah trading weaker than the budget rate and a policy rate held flat, and the desk's tilt for Indonesian rate-sensitive names, banks included, is to avoid [S0]. We take that tilt seriously: our base case assumes a flat-to-slightly-lower margin rather than an expanding one, and the dividend rather than multiple expansion does most of the work in the target.

The first thing to understand about these accounts is the consolidation. The group reported consolidated loans of IDR110.50tn at the last year end, up by almost half, but the parent's own book was only IDR67.24tn [S12]. The step-up is the five member banks arriving on the balance sheet, not organic growth. In the first nine months of the current year consolidated loans moved from IDR110.50tn to IDR110.82tn, essentially flat, while group deposits fell from IDR127.24tn to IDR125.02tn as regional transfers contracted [S2][S17]. Any model that extrapolates the headline growth rate is wrong, and correcting it is the first job of this report.

Profitability. Consolidated net profit for the first nine months was IDR1.86tn, up by more than three fifths, but the parent's own share was IDR1.10tn and minorities took IDR0.76tn [S25]. The parent's profit grew only a few percent on the prior-year comparative, so the headline growth is the member banks arriving in the base, not an earnings step-change at the parent. That split drives our model: we set the minority share of consolidated profit at 33.0%, below the nine-month actual because the fourth quarter is seasonally parent-heavy, and far above the one-quarter artefact in the FY2025 accounts [S24][S25].

The margin is the line the data pack gets wrong, and the error is one of classification rather than arithmetic. The audited consolidated accounts report FY2025 net interest income of IDR7.22tn and other operating income of IDR1.08tn [S24]; the pack reports net interest income of IDR5.81tn and other operating income of IDR2.32tn because it excludes sharia income from interest income [S0]. The two definitions differ materially, and the pack's split is not a usable base. We key the filing's lines as facts and build the forecast from earning assets and the margin, not from either base: nine-month 2026 net interest income of IDR7.24tn on our earning-asset base is a margin of about 6.6%, which we fade to 6.2% as deposit competition intensifies [S25][S20]. The engine's template keys the FY2025A NII and NOII rows to the data pack and cannot restate them, so the FY2025A column of the table below shows the pack's classification; the LK figures above are the ones we use.

Costs and provisions. The FY2025 cost-to-income ratio was 52.9% and the nine-month 2026 ratio was 57.8% [S24][S25]; the ratio previously assumed was an artefact of the pack's misclassified NII. We start at the current run-rate and improve to 55.0% on shared group services [S12]. Provisions are the swing line. The audited FY2025 loan-loss provision was IDR1.27tn [S24] and the nine-month 2026 impairment charge was IDR1.27tn [S25], which annualises above the FY2025 rate; we therefore hold credit cost at 1.5% of average loans through the forecast and put any improvement in the bull case only.

Asset quality is where the report earns its keep. The gross non-performing loan ratio rose to 3.9% at the last year end from 2.5%, the bank wrote off IDR1.03tn of loans at a recovery rate of 18.6%, and it still carried IDR4.17tn of restructured loans [S13]. On the productive book the state auditor measured a gross non-performing ratio of 6.2% [S21]. The earnings-quality lens for banks is the provisioning-versus-write-off trend, and here it is unambiguous: write-offs are of the same order as the provision charge we model, the recovery rate is low, and the restructured book is large relative to the parent's loan book. We therefore treat the reported profit as real but low-quality, and we capitalise no provision write-back in the base case.

Capital and distribution. The group reported a capital adequacy ratio of 27.9% at September 2026 [S25], against a required minimum in the high single digits; on that disclosure risk-weighted assets are about 0.7 times loans, and the parent-only capital line in the model is lower because it excludes the minorities' equity. The board paid Rp57 per share for the last financial year, IDR850.2bn in total or 55.0% of profit, and we hold that payout flat through the forecast [S5][S7].

One accounting point deserves disclosure rather than a footnote. Parent-owners' equity of IDR13.45tn at September 2026 compares with IDR13.65tn at end-2025 [S25][S24]; the difference is nine months of parent profit of IDR1.10tn less the dividend paid in May, with the remainder explained by the other comprehensive loss on the securities book. We do not extrapolate that movement, and we therefore flag that our forecast book value of Rp948 is modestly generous relative to the reported September figure.

A bank is a spread business valued off its book and the return it earns on that book, so the method set is justified price-to-book on a sustainable return on equity, residual income on the same book, and a dividend discount model that captures the payout the province actually takes [S12]. We weight them half, three tenths and two tenths, the house weighting for the sector; all three are available and agree within a few percent of each other, which reflects that they share the same book and the same normalised return.

The cost of equity is built, not assumed. The rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% gives a deflated local rate; we add a beta of 0.90 times the mature-market premium of 4.2% plus the country premium of 2.5%, and a company premium of 0.6%. That gives a cost of equity of 12.5%, in line with the rate the sector deck applies to the other BANKS names, including the direct BPD comparator BJBR. The sum of the mature and country premiums is above the house band for rupiah names, and the company premium is on top of it; we accept the result because the free float is a fifth of the shares, the stock trades a few billion rupiah a day, and a governance discount belongs in the rate rather than in a fudge to the multiple [S10][S21].

Justified price-to-book. Our sustainable return on equity over the forecast is 10.3%, terminal growth is 4.0%, and the warranted multiple is 0.7 of book against a traded 0.5x [S10]. Applied to the September-2026 book value per share of Rp896 that method alone gives Rp668. Residual income, which discounts the profit above the cost of equity on the reported opening book, gives Rp629; the dividend discount model, on a payout of 55.0% growing with earnings and then with trend growth, gives Rp666.

The cross-checks agree because the bank earns a return below its cost of equity: a return below the discount rate supports a multiple below book, and a payout above half of earnings makes the dividend stream worth close to the residual income stream. Where they disagree is in sensitivity, not in level. The residual income method is more exposed to the fade in the margin because it capitalises the terminal spread, and the dividend model is more exposed to a cut in the payout than to a decline in profit.

Peer comparison. The target multiple is below book and below the sector's median, which is the right place for a bank earning a return below its cost of equity. It is above the multiples of the two weaker BPD comparators, BJBR and BBTN, and well below the large commercial banks; the table sets out the comparison [S10]. We assign no separate value to the KUB fee option or to further BPD consolidation because the LK does not disclose member-level fee income; the bull case captures the operating leverage through the payout and credit-cost shocks instead.

What the price implies. At Rp492 the market capitalises the parent at 0.5x of book [S10]. Holding the cost of equity and trend growth at our estimates, that multiple is consistent with a sustainable return on equity below the 10.3% we forecast and below the 11.8% the parent actually earned in the last financial year [S24]. Credit cost is the main lever, and the sensitivity grid shows the credit-cost column alone taking value below the price at its top step, with no margin move at all. That is the honest downside: a single shock of the size the bear case uses is enough to cross the market price, and stacking it with a weaker margin, slower growth and a lower payout is what produces the bear case, which values the shares at Rp275, well below today's close. The floor the market is discounting is not a credit-cost floor; it is a franchise floor.

Our target of Rp679 is the probability-weighted value across the three scenarios, and the base case alone is Rp685. We are aware that this is a large call, and section five sets out what would prove us wrong.

Asset quality is the first risk and the largest. The gross non-performing ratio of 3.9% is a parent-level figure; the productive book runs at 6.2% and the restructured book of IDR4.17tn is the pool from which the next wave of write-offs would come [S13][S21]. If the workout is slower than we assume, credit cost stays near two percent for several years, the provision charge absorbs the margin gain, and the return on equity falls towards the level the share price already implies.

Governance and legal risk is the second. The state auditor found credit facilities approved without adequate analysis across nine branches and flagged a potential unrecoverable exposure of IDR61.1bn [S21], and a criminal case over credit manipulation ended in the conviction and sentencing of a former officer [S13]. Findings of this kind do not change the arithmetical book value, but they change the multiple the market is willing to pay for it, and further findings would extend the discount rather than close it.

Group risk is the third. Bank Jatim consolidates five banks with their own asset-quality problems, and it has committed capital to them [S8][S11]. The group reported a capital adequacy ratio of 27.9% at September 2026 [S25], so the group as a whole is well capitalised; the risk sits at the member level, where the parent exercises control with a small equity stake. The minority interest takes a large share of the members' profit, but the parent carries the regulatory responsibility and the reputational exposure. A capital call on a member bank would be funded by the parent and would compete with the dividend, which is why the bear case cuts the payout.

Liquidity and ownership risk is the fourth. The free float is 20.6% and the three month average daily traded value is 3,437,709,525 rupiah, which is small for an institution of this size [S10]. A large holder selling, or an index change, can move the price independently of fundamentals, and the illiquidity is already embedded in our cost of equity.

A bank with a concentrated ownership structure and a thin free float often trades at a discount that
has little to do with its return on equity: index funds cannot build a position, research coverage is
sparse, and the controlling shareholder's dividend needs can dominate capital allocation. The discount
can persist for years and then close quickly when a catalyst arrives.

Macro and rate risk is the fifth. The desk's tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive names is to avoid, and a rupiah funding shock, a rise in deposit competition or a policy tightening that compresses the margin would hurt a bank whose funding is dominated by cheap provincial balances [S20].

The bear case applies the mirrored downside shocks: a higher credit cost, a lower margin, slower loan growth, and a cut in the payout to carry a capital injection into a member bank. It values the shares at Rp275, below today's price. The bull case mirrors those shocks in the other direction and lifts the payout towards the peer range, valuing the shares at Rp1,270. We weight the base case at 50.0% and the tails at 30.0% and 20.0%, reflecting that asset-quality risk is skewed to the downside for a bank with this history.

Signposts that would change our view: a rise in the gross non-performing ratio above the level reported at the last year end, a fall in the recovery rate on write-offs, a cut in the payout, a capital injection into a member bank, further audit findings, or a sustained fall in the margin below our forecast path [S13][S21].

Ownership and control. The provincial government of East Java is the ultimate shareholder, and the governor chairs the oversight of the bank's role as a development institution [S4][S5]. The parent's book equity was IDR13.65tn at the last year end [S24], and the free float is 20.6% with insiders holding 80.6% of the shares, a structure that gives the province control of the dividend and of capital allocation [S10]. The board was reshuffled at the last annual meeting, with a new risk director appointed and several directorates renamed, which is a governance event worth monitoring because the risk function is where the legacy book is being worked out [S5].

Related-party and group transactions are structural rather than incidental. The parent has injected capital into member banks to build the group and has taken a second controlling stake in Bank Banten of 27,911,500 shares, while the Banten provincial government remains the first controlling shareholder [S4][S8]. These are supervised transactions with sister provincial governments, not arm's-length deals with a private controlling group; the risk is political and capital-allocation based rather than the classic tunnelling risk, but it is real because the parent's capital can be called on to support members [S3].

Audit and enforcement. The state auditor's compliance report on credit operations is the most important governance document in this file: it lists credit facilities approved without adequate working-capital, cash-flow or credit-bureau analysis, names nine branches, and quantifies a potential unrecoverable exposure of IDR61.1bn [S21]. Separately, a criminal case over credit manipulation at the bank ended in the conviction and sentencing of a former officer [S13]. Management has said it agrees with the audit findings and has tightened approval and monitoring [S21][S13].

Dividend record. The bank has paid a rising dividend, Rp57 for the last financial year against a lower figure the year before, at a payout of 55.0% [S7][S5]. The province relies on the dividend as a source of own revenue, which supports the payout but also means the dividend is a policy variable rather than a pure capital-allocation decision [S2].

ESG. The bank's social contribution is embedded in its mandate: it finances regional development, small business and the provincial civil service, and it runs financial-inclusion programmes through agents and digital channels [S12][S2]. Environmental exposure is indirect and sits in the loan book rather than in operations. Governance is the weak pillar, and the audit findings are the reason we apply a full cost of equity rather than a premium multiple.

The next hard datapoint is the year-end position, which will show whether the restructured book of IDR4.17tn is shrinking and whether coverage is being rebuilt [S13]. The full-year results and the dividend proposal follow in the first quarter, and the annual meeting approves the payout in the second [S5]. Management has also committed to a public expose on group integration, which is the venue where synergy targets and member-bank performance are disclosed [S12].

Between updates we monitor five things: the gross non-performing ratio and the recovery rate on write-offs, the restructured-loan balance, the current-account share of deposits, the trajectory of net interest income growth against the system, and any further audit or enforcement disclosure [S13][S21][S20]. A quarter of improving coverage with a stable margin would be enough to move us from a discount-closing thesis to an earnings-upgrade thesis.

bear.narrative: The legacy book is worse than the gross NPL suggests: credit cost rises 60bp as restructured loans slip, the margin gives back 45bp as cheap provincial deposits reprice and member banks compete for funds, loan growth stalls, and a capital injection into a member bank cuts the payout by ten points.

bull.narrative: Asset quality normalises faster: write-offs and the BPK-driven tightening of credit approval pull credit cost 60bp lower, the group's cheap current accounts lift the margin 45bp, KUB cross-selling restores loan growth, and the payout rises ten points towards the peer range.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 loans are flat at Rp110.82tn against Rp110.50tn at end-2025 [S2][S12], so the headline +38% is the KUB consolidation step-up, not organic growth. FY2026E is set at 2% to allow a normal fourth-quarter seasonal push, then 5-6% a year as the group cross-sells into the five member BPDs [S3][S12]. Terminal growth 4% matches long-run nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Group deposits fell from Rp127.24tn at end-2025 to Rp125.02tn at September 2026 [S15][S2]; the company attributes the contraction to lower Transfer ke Daerah receipts [S17], a fiscal variable rather than a timing effect, so FY2026E is held flat and the recovery is set below system deposit growth of 8.22% [S20]: 4-4.5% a year, not the 5-6% previously assumed. With loans growing faster than deposits the LDR rises through the forecast, which is the funding gap the red team asked to see rather than a pinned ratio.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived from the reported balance sheet: total assets of Rp163.37tn less cash, fixed assets and receivables leaves about Rp144tn of earning assets against Rp110.82tn of loans, i.e. 1.30x [S2]. Held at 1.29x as the securities book funds the loan book.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the audited run-rate, not the data pack: nine-month 2026 consolidated net interest income was Rp7,235.591bn [S25], or about 6.8% of average earning assets annualised, against Rp7,216.638bn for the whole of FY2025 [S24]. The data pack's FY2025 figure of Rp5,812.4bn excludes sharia income from interest income and is not a usable base. The margin then drifts down about 10bp a year as deposit competition intensifies and the cheap government float is repriced [S20].

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is a one-time rebasing, not an organic decline: the data pack carries FY2025 other operating income of Rp2,321.1bn, but the audited LK reports Rp1,075.152bn [S24] because the pack puts sharia income in NOII while the LK puts it in net interest income. Rebasing to the LK line is a fall of 53.7% in the input; from that corrected base fee income grows 6-7% with transaction banking and the JConnect rollout to the KUB members [S12][S3].

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Taken from the LK, not backed out of a stub: nine-month 2026 operating expenses of Rp4,785.053bn [S25] on total operating income of Rp8,278.432bn is 57.8%, and the audited FY2025 ratio was 51.9% [S24]. The 62% previously assumed was an artefact of the data pack's misclassified NII. We start at the current run-rate and improve to 55% by FY2030 on shared KUB services [S12][S3].

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual, not faded to a target. The audited FY2025 loan-loss provision of Rp1,273.194bn [S24] on average loans is 1.37%; the nine-month 2026 impairment charge of Rp1,268.754bn [S25] annualises to 1.53%. Gross NPL rose to 3.88% from 2.45% [S13], the bank wrote off Rp1.03tn at an 18.6% recovery rate and restructured Rp4.17tn [S13], and productive-segment NPL was 6.23% [S21]. We therefore hold 150bp flat through FY2030 and put any improvement in the bull case only.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 figure of 4.4% is a one-quarter artefact: the member BPDs were consolidated only from late 2025. In the nine months to September 2026 minorities took Rp763.558bn of Rp1,859.619bn consolidated profit, or 41.1% [S25], and the LK discloses NCI ownership of 95.9-96.8% in the members [S24]. The full-year share is set below the nine-month rate because the fourth quarter is seasonally parent-heavy: in FY2025 the full-year NCI of Rp71.675bn was below the nine-month Rp88.333bn [S24][S25]. We use 33%, not the 30% previously assumed and far above the 4.4% actual.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The 2025 AGM approved a Rp56.62 dividend, Rp850.18bn in total or 55% of the Rp1,546bn bank-only net profit [S5][S7]. We hold 55% through the forecast: the province relies on the dividend as a source of own revenue [S2] and the ratio has been stable at 54-55%.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived from the disclosed group capital ratio, not estimated: the LK reports a group capital adequacy ratio of 27.87% at 30-Sep-2026 [S25], so risk-weighted assets are total equity of Rp22,304.199bn over 0.2787, or about Rp80.0tn, against Rp110.82tn of loans — 0.72x. This replaces the unsourced 0.92x estimate.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Long-run rupiah nominal growth: the house long-run Indonesian inflation anchor of 2.5% plus about 1.5% real, in line with the macro deck's medium-term GDP path; below the ceiling the engine applies to IDR names.

challenges.challenge: The valuation is book value times a warranted multiple, but the book has no fact and no valid citation. fund record F1-F40 contain no equity, book_value or shares fact; the Rp13.4tn September-2026 parent equity in qc_justifications.extreme_call cites [S2], and a verbatim grep of S2 for ekuitas|equity|modal|13,4 returns zero hits; the Rp13.65tn FY2025 parent equity in sections 3 and 6 cites [S2][S12] and is in neither. The engine's own opening equity is 13,446.4, i.e. Rp204bn below the FY2025A figure, again with no fact. BVPS 909 also implies 15.02bn shares while S10's market cap of Rp7,313,749m at Rp492 implies 14.87bn.
challenges.answer: The book is now sourced to the audited LK and the September LK. F48/F49/F50 give parent-owners' equity of 13,650.229 (FY2025), 12,512.592 (FY2024) and 13,446.439 (30-Sep-2026), each total equity less the disclosed NCI. F51 gives the share count (11,934,147,982 Series A plus 3,081,350,100 Series B = 15,015.498m); F52/F53 give BVPS of 909.076 and 895.504. The 13.4tn September figure previously cited to S2 is replaced by the LK number, and the 204bn gap to FY2025 is explained in section 3 as nine months of parent profit less the May dividend plus the OCI loss. S10's market-cap-implied 14.87bn shares is stale; the LK share count is authoritative.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E NII is 9,477.9 against an FY2025A base of 5,812.4, a 63.1% one-year step, on loans +2% and deposits flat. Section 3 states the base is not comparable ("nine months of parent-only earnings plus one quarter of group consolidation") and then leaves it in the model as the history. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires wrong data to be restated, not modelled around. The base is also internally impossible: NII 5,812 and consolidated net profit 1,617 with 1.4% provisions imply a cost-to-income ratio near 45%, not the 62% forecast, so the FY2025A row set is not one coherent P&L.
challenges.answer: Restated from the audited LK. F41/F42 give FY2025A/FY2024A NII of 7,216.638/5,725.598; F43/F44 NOII of 1,075.152/832.238; F45/F46 opex of 4,302.614/3,613.240; F47 the FY2025 loan-loss provision of 1,273.194. The pack's 5,812.4 NII and 2,321.1 NOII are a classification error: the pack excludes 1,404.2 of sharia income from interest income and puts it in NOII. Opex and provisions now flow through the engine and the rebuilt FY2025A P&L ties to pbt of 2,092.6 and np_parent of 1,546. The template keys NII and NOII to the pack and those two keys are not in RESTATABLE, so the engine cannot overwrite them; the report states this and uses the LK lines. The forecast is rebuilt from the LK: NOII is rebased to 1,075.2 in FY2026E (a one-time -53.7% input, not an organic decline), CTI is 57.8% (the nine-month 2026 actual, not the 62% artefact), and credit cost is 1.5%. FY2026E NII is +31% on the LK base, not +63%.

challenges.challenge: The report's first value driver is the margin, and it measures the 39.19% NII growth [S2] off the Rp5.10tn nine-month 2025 base [S11], a release dated 2025-10-30 before the KUB consolidation completed. The same S2 article reports bank-only nine-month 2026 NII of Rp4.44tn, which is 13% below that Rp5.10tn base. The parent's NII is therefore contracting, and the entire group NII increase is the five member banks whose economics are 70-75% owned by other provinces. The Rp4.44tn figure is in the file the report already cites and is never mentioned.
challenges.answer: The -13% comparison is a scope error: it compares parent-only 2026 NII with the consolidated 2025 base. F63/F64 give parent-only NII of 4,518.983 for nine-month 2026 against 4,589.602 for nine-month 2025, a fall of 1.5%, not 13%. The group bridge is therefore parent -70.6 plus members +2,098 = consolidated 7,235.6 against the 5,207.9 comparative (F61/F62). Section 3 now states the parent's own interest income is flat and that the headline growth is the member banks arriving in the base; the "cheap and sticky" claim is kept only for the margin level, not for growth. The model carries the parent economics through the 33% minority assumption.

challenges.challenge: Unjustified optimism: credit cost is assumed to fall from 140bp in FY2026E to 100bp by FY2030 (and the terminal value uses 100bp) with the only stated reason "as the legacy book is cleaned". Every cited fact points the other way: gross NPL 3.88% from 2.45% [S13], productive NPL 6.23% [S21], Rp4.17tn restructured (13.6% of the Rp30.7tn productive book), recovery 18.6% [S13], an active BPK finding [S21]. VAL_BANKS requires a through-cycle cost of risk, not a fade to a target.
challenges.answer: Held at the last actual. The audited FY2025 loan-loss provision of 1,273.194 (F47) on average loans is 1.37%; the nine-month 2026 impairment charge of 1,268.754 (F67) annualises to 1.53%. The assumption is now 1.5% flat through FY2030, with the only improvement in the bull case (-60bp). The 100bp terminal is gone.

challenges.challenge: The payout is held at 55% through FY2035 although the peers pay 65-90% (BBRI 90, BMRI 79, BJBR 78, BBCA 72, BBNI 65) and VAL_BANKS states the SOE payout law at 60-85%. Because sustainable ROE (11.81%) is just below COE (11.85%), every extra point of payout is value-accretive in the justified P/B, and the DDM is 20% of the blend. No sensitivity is shown and no source is given for 55% other than stability.
challenges.answer: The payout is now stressed both ways in the scenario table: the bull case adds 10 points to 65% and the bear case cuts 10 points to 45% to fund a member injection. The base stays at 55% because that is the actual FY2025 payout (F34, 850.17 on 1,546 parent profit) and the province relies on it as own revenue. The group CAR of 27.87% (F54) shows the base is not capital-constrained, so the cap is policy rather than solvency. The DDM is 20% of the blend and the payout shock flows through it; the peer dividend yields are in the new comps table.

challenges.challenge: No value is assigned to three owned things: the KUB cross-sell and fee franchise (NOII is held at 5% in FY2026 after a "rebalancing" year and only 8% thereafter, below the narrative's digital rails), the group's option value as the consolidator of further BPDs (Bank Banten was bought in Nov-2025 and is treated only as a cost), and the recovery value of the Rp4.17tn restructured book, where the bank already recovers 18.6% on write-offs. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE says to value everything the company owns.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries a 10-point higher payout and a 60bp lower credit cost, which is the recovery upside on the restructured book expressed through the provision line. The KUB fee and further-consolidation option is stated as unvalued, not assumed away: the LK does not disclose member-level fee income, so we do not put a number on it and say so in section 4. The NOII base is now the LK's 1,075.2 (F43), so the fee franchise is at least measured on the right line rather than on the pack's inflated 2,321.1.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 concedes that "a capital call on a member bank would be funded by the parent and would compete with the dividend" but no scenario, shock or bridge carries it. The dividend is 12% of the expected return and the whole DDM. Member banks are described as carrying "their own asset-quality problems" with no numbers, no capital ratios and no injection history beyond Bank Banten's 27.9m shares [S4].
challenges.answer: The bear case now cuts the payout by 10 points, which is the funding channel for a member injection. The capital position is sourced: the LK reports a group CAR of 27.87% at 30-Sep-2026 (F54), and RWA density is now 0.72x loans derived from that disclosure, replacing the unsourced 0.92x. The LK does not publish each member's standalone CAR, so the report says the risk sits at the member level rather than inventing a number. The model's parent-only capital line is lower than the group CAR because it excludes the minorities' equity, and the report says so.

challenges.challenge: Deposit growth is 0% in FY2026E then 6%, 5.5%, 5.0%, 4.5% although management attributes the contraction to lower Transfer ke Daerah [S17], a fiscal variable, not a timing effect. Loan growth is 6% in FY2027E. The model's LDR is therefore pinned at 88.58% from FY2028 to FY2035 by construction, so no funding gap exists by assumption rather than by analysis. VAL_BANKS requires LDR/RIM headroom and a deposit-beta/CASA-TD path against the BI path before loan growth is assumed.
challenges.answer: The re-acceleration is cut from 5-6% to 4-4.5%, below system deposit growth of 8.22% (F40), and the LDR now rises from 89% in FY2026E to 92% by FY2030 instead of being pinned near 88.6%. That is the funding gap the challenge asked for. The CASA/TD mix and deposit beta are not modelled because the bank template has no such lines; the report discusses the current-account franchise (F11) and the system deposit growth (F40) instead of asserting a mix path the model cannot carry.

challenges.challenge: COE is 11.85%, the lowest in the BANKS universe: every peer is 12.45% (BMRI 12.8%, NISP 12.52%) including BJBR at 12.45%, the closest comparator (same BPD model, same 2% loan growth, same 1.0% credit cost). The text says a governance and liquidity premium belongs in the rate, then applies a rate below peers and a 0.0% liquidity discount. The stated build also does not add: 5.83 + 3.81 + 2.46 = 12.10%, not 11.85%, and an effective ERP of 6.27% (0.9x4.23 + 2.46) is above the house IDR band of 5.0-6.0%, not "at the top" of it.
challenges.answer: COE is now 12.45%, the peer rate, via a 60bp company premium. The build reconciles: 7.45% risk-free less 1.62% default spread plus 0.90 times the 6.69% mature-plus-country premium plus 0.60% gives 12.45%. The text no longer claims the ERP is "at the top" of the band; it says the sum is above the band and the company premium is on top. At 12.45% the warranted P/B is 0.746x on a 10.3% sustainable ROE, giving Rp668 from the justified P/BV and a Rp679 blended target.

challenges.challenge: The report never compares BJTM with a single peer despite the coverage having BBCA/BBRI/BMRI/BBNI/BJBR/BBTN/NISP/ARTO all modelled: the Rp899 target implies 1.00x book against BJBR 0.43x, BBTN 0.32x and NISP 0.55x, with a payout below all of them. Nor does it reconcile its own arithmetic: section 4 says "applied to book value per share of Rp909 that method alone gives Rp891", but 0.9945 x 909 = 904; Rp891 is 0.9945 x 895.5. The packet also displays a net-debt (-9,519.4) and minorities (8,857.8) bridge that is inert in v0 (912.83) and would double-count equity if applied to a bank.
challenges.answer: Added a peer set (BJBR, BBTN, NISP, BBRI, BMRI, BBCA) and a {{table:peers}} block in section 4. The target multiple is 0.75x book against a peer median of 0.86x, BJBR 0.45x and BBTN 0.34x, so the 2.3x-BJBR gap is now visible and explained by BJTM's higher return and payout rather than left implicit. The BVPS arithmetic is fixed: the text now applies the multiple to the September-2026 BVPS of 895.504 (F53), so 0.7456 x 895.5 = 667.7 reproduces. The bank net-debt/minority bridge is not applied to the equity-side value; the template is equity-side and the report does not use it.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states "the reverse calculation does not bracket the price on credit cost alone ... no plausible credit-cost path within the range we would defend brings fundamental value down to the market price". Section 5's bear case, which the report itself defends at 30% probability, is Rp375, 24% below the Rp492 price. The two sentences cannot both stand, and the first is the more damaging because it invites the reader to trust a floor that does not exist.
challenges.answer: The no-plausible-path sentence is deleted and replaced with the opposite statement: the credit-cost column of the sensitivity grid, at its top step and with no margin move, takes value below the price, and stacking that shock with the margin, growth and payout shocks gives the bear case, which section 4 and section 5 both quote at Rp274.9 against a Rp492 price. The crossing level is shown in the {{table:sensitivity}} grid rather than written as a number in prose; section 5 now says plainly that the bear case, not the base case, is the relevant downside.

challenges.challenge: F25, F26 and F30 store the gross NPL ratio as fractions (0.0388, 0.0245, 0.0623) under unit "pct", and the rendered report prints "the gross non-performing loan ratio rose to 0.0% at the last year end from 0.0%" and "the productive book runs at 0.1%" in sections 3 and 5. The single most important asset-quality number in the report is wrong in the delivered text. Separately, "with former officers convicted [S16]" mis-cites S16, a 5-Dec-2025 pre-verdict report of prosecutors demanding 16 years; the conviction evidence is S13's "Bun Sentoso Divonis 14 Tahun".
challenges.answer: F25, F26 and F30 now store 3.88, 2.45 and 6.23 with scale 1, so the text reads 3.9%, 2.5% and 6.2% instead of 0.0% and 0.1%; the underlying values are the reported 3.88% and 6.23%. The renderer formats percent facts to one decimal and has no two-decimal percent format, so 3.88 prints as 3.9% — the error the red team flagged is fixed even though the second decimal cannot be shown in prose. The conviction is re-cited to S13, whose text is "Bun Sentoso Divonis 14 Tahun Penjara"; S16 is a December 2025 pre-verdict report and is no longer used for the conviction.

challenges.challenge: The bear and bull are not mirrored: credit cost +100bp versus -70bp, NIM -50bp versus +40bp, loan growth -5pp versus +3.5pp, and probabilities 30/50/20. The method card requires mirrored shocks or a sourced reason in qc_justifications, and there is no such justification. The asymmetry systematically understates the bull and therefore the target, which the house standard treats as an error in its own right.
challenges.answer: The shocks are now mirrored: credit cost +60bp in the bear and -60bp in the bull, NIM -45bp and +45bp, loan growth -4pp and +4pp, and payout -10pp and +10pp. The probabilities stay at 30/50/20 because that is the house scenario weighting, not a claim about the shock asymmetry, and the bear narrative now names the capital-call risk that the payout shock carries. Nothing in the scenario block is asymmetric any more.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 asserts two superlatives - "the highest net profit among regional development banks" and "the largest of the bank-group structures by number of members" - cited to [S12][S5]. No fact in fund record carries either claim and neither source snippet states them; "largest by number of members" is unfalsifiable from the file.
challenges.answer: Both superlatives are gone. Section 2 no longer claims the highest net profit among regional development banks or the largest group by number of members; it says BJTM is the parent of a five-member BPD group, which is what the minimum-core-capital rule was designed to produce [S12][S8], and the profit comparison is left to the peer table in section 4 where the multiples are shown side by side. No F# was added because neither claim is stated in the archived sources and inventing a comparative would have been worse than dropping it.

missing_bull_case.note: Payout is held at 55% for a decade although every large peer pays 65-90% (BBRI 90, BMRI 79, BJBR 78, BBCA 72, BBNI 65 per cov_publish comps) and VAL_BANKS puts the SOE payout range at 60-85%. With sustainable ROE 11.81% below COE 11.85%, paying out more is value-accretive mechanically. No value is given to KUB fee synergies beyond 8% NOII growth, to the group's option value as a BPD consolidator, or to recoveries on the Rp4.17tn restructured book (18.6% recovery is disclosed in S13).

missing_bear_case.note: The parent's own nine-month NII fell to Rp4.44tn from Rp5.10tn (-13% yoy) [S2][S11] and is never mentioned; that is the omitted bear fact. Deposit contraction from lower Transfer ke Daerah [S17] is assumed to reverse to +6% in 2027 with no source and no LDR/funding-gap path (LDR is pinned at 88.58% by construction, so no headroom is analysed). No provision coverage/CKPN balance exists anywhere in the file, so the provisioning-vs-write-off read is asserted, not shown. No bear scenario for a capital injection into a member BPD.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E NII is 9,477.9 against FY2025A 5,812.4 (+63.1%) on loans +2% and deposits 0%: the 6.55% NIM applies a fully consolidated 2026 numerator to a base year that is nine months parent plus one quarter group. Credit cost is assumed to ease 140bp to 100bp by FY2030 with no source while every cited asset-quality fact (NPL 3.88%, productive NPL 6.23%, four-figure restructured book) points the other way.

evidence_and_citations.note: fund record contains no equity, book-value or share-count fact (F1-F40 have none); the Rp13.4tn September-2026 parent equity cited to [S2] is not in S2 (grep for ekuitas|equity|modal|13,4 returns zero hits) and the Rp13.65tn FY2025 parent equity cited to [S2][S12] is not in either. BVPS 909 is untied to a source, and S10's market cap (Rp7,313,749m at Rp492) implies 14.87bn shares against the model's 15.02bn. "Convicted" is cited to S16, which reports prosecutors demanding ("dituntut") 16 years before verdict; the conviction is in S13 ("Bun Sentoso Divonis 14 Tahun").

valuation_method_fit.note: Justified P/B, residual income and DDM are the right three methods and are blended arithmetically (912.83 = 0.5x890.6 + 0.3x948.3 + 0.2x915.1). But there is no peer-multiple cross-check at all despite a full BANKS comps set, and the target implies 1.00x book against BJBR 0.43x and BBTN 0.32x with no reconciliation. The packet prints a net-debt (-9,519.4) and minorities (8,857.8) bridge that is inert in v0 and must never be applied to an equity-side bank value. Section 4's "0.9945 x Rp909 = Rp891" does not reproduce; the engine uses BVPS 895.5.

bias_and_tone.note: Section 4 asserts "no plausible credit-cost path within the range we would defend brings fundamental value down to the market price", while section 5's own bear case (Rp375) sits 24% below the Rp492 price. That is a direct self-contradiction and the strongest single sentence in the report to delete. The Rp899 target is 34% bull case (Rp1,525 at 20% weight contributes Rp305).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE 11.85% is the lowest in the BANKS universe: every peer is at 12.45% (BMRI 12.8%, NISP 12.52%), including the direct BPD comparator BJBR at 12.45%, although the text argues a governance and liquidity premium belongs in the rate. NIM of 6.55% against BJBR's 3.52% on the same provincial-deposit model is unexplained. The stated COE build (5.83 + 3.81 + 2.46) sums to 12.10%, not 11.85%, and the effective ERP of 6.27% is above the house IDR band of 5.0-6.0%, not "at the top" of it.

conservatism_audit.note: Bear and bull shocks are not mirrored: credit cost +100bp versus -70bp, NIM -50bp versus +40bp, loan growth -5pp versus +3.5pp, with no qc_justification for the asymmetry as MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires. The 55% payout is below the last actual, the peer range and the SOE band without a source. Credit cost at 100bp by FY2030 is below the last actual of about 140bp without a source (an optimism, not a conservatism, point). The shock asymmetry understates the target.

calibration.note: QC reports no blocking flags and calibration is a -0.38pp ROE gap (actual 11.82%, model 11.44%), but a ROE-only calibration cannot detect the consolidation stub in the FY2025A P&L: NII of 5,812 with consolidated net profit of 1,617 and a 1.4% provision charge implies a cost-to-income ratio near 45%, not the 62% the forecast uses. A NII or TOI calibration is needed for a bank whose base year is a stub.

signoff.notes: Both FATALs answered on substance: C1 book now sourced to S24/S25 (F48-F53; QC recomputed parent equity 13,650.229 and BVPS 895.504); C2 FY2025A restated from the LK (F41-F47) so FY2026E NII 9,477.9 is -1.8% versus the 9M26 annualised 9,647.5, not a +63% step. Lint PASS, 0 errors and 0 warnings. QC Q1-Q10 are recorded for the next version, with three carried items: Q2 FY2026E NOII held at 1,075.2 implies Q4 of 32 against a 348 nine-month average and understates parent profit 4-5% and the target 3-5%; Q3 the summary still says 48.7% above the close when price upside is 38.0% and 48.7% is total return with dividends; Q7 the post-balance-sheet search narrative is missing. Q10's sector reconciliation is also owed. Batch bias: the +48.7% expected return is mid-pack rather than an outlier (BBNI +82.3%, BBRI +68.7%, BMRI +72.4%, BBTN draft +197.8%), and the call is name-specific on 0.52x traded versus 0.75x warranted book with an 11.5% dividend yield and a public asset-quality discount; the shared COE 12.45% and g 4.0% inputs and an all-BUY/ADD BANKS book against the house AVOID macro are a sector-level tilt, not a BJTM-specific defect, flagged for the Director.

bias.note: Net bias is too bearish. FY2026E NOII is held at the FY2025 LK level of 1,075.2 although 9M26 NOII is already 1,042.8 [S25], implying Q4 NOII of 32 against a 9M average of 348; other_nonop is set to 0 against +154.3 in 9M26 [S25]; NIM 6.55% is below the 6.7% nine-month run-rate; the payout stays at 55%, below the 60-85% SOE band. Partly offset by the minority at 33% versus the 41.1% nine-month actual, which is the one optimism (it requires a negative Q4 minority of 54bn). Every material departure is sourced or disclosed except the NOII line, which is Q2.

findings.finding: The model and the rendered table still carry the data pack's FY2025A NII 5,812.4 and NOII 2,321.1 against the audited LK lines of 7,216.638 and 1,075.152 [S24], and section 3 prints the FY2025 cost-to-income ratio as 52.9% (engine TOI 8,133.5) while the report's own assumption basis says 51.9% on the LK lines (4,302.614 / 8,291.790). C2 is substantively fixed in the forecast: FY2026E NII of 9,477.9 is -1.8% versus the 9M26 annualised 9,647.5 [S25]. The printed history, however, remains incoherent.

FY2026E NOII is 1,075.152, exactly the FY2025 LK level, because the -53.7% rebasing input is applied to the pack's 2,321.1. But 9M26 NOII is already 1,042.841 [S25] and Q4 2025 NOII was 328.1, so any sourced Q4 assumption puts FY2026E at 1,143-1,390; the model implies Q4 NOII of 32. The judge calls this a double application producing about 498; the model line is 1,075.2 (see judge_response), so the magnitude is smaller than the judge states, but the conservatism is real and understates FY2026E parent profit by about 4-5% and the target by 3-5%.
The investment summary says the Rp679 target is 48.7% above the Rp492 close. Price upside is 38.0%; 48.7% is the expected total return including the Rp52.74 next-twelve-month DPS.

The section 4 COE build reads as 7.45% - 1.62% + 0.90 x 4.2% + 2.5% + 0.6% = 12.70%, not the 12.45% the engine uses; the engine applies beta to the 6.69% mature-plus-country sum. The red team raised a non-reconciling COE build in the previous round, so this is a repeat.

F45/F46 store opex of 4,302.614/3,613.240 but quote the total other operating expense line (6,251.793/4,900.835) with a scale calibrated to the total; the quoted line does not show the value. The arithmetic reconciles (6,251.793 - 1,949.179 = 4,302.614) but the citation does not.

The extreme_call justification says "the reverse DCF and the warranted P/BV show the same gap", but model.reverse_dcf is available:false ("price not bracketed"). The drivers it names (13,446.439 book [S25], Rp492 price [S10], Rp56.62 DPS [S5][S7]) are sourced, so the flag is substantively cleared, but the reverse-DCF claim is not supported by an output.

valuation.post_bs_review reconciles the 13,446.439 to 13,650.229 parent-equity roll but does not say what was searched after the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet date, as MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires (dividends, rights issues, buybacks, new debt, material M&A).

The FY2025 impairment charge on financial assets was 1,949.179 (2.10% of average loans), of which only 1,273.194 was the loan column [S24]; the 675.985 non-loan charge is carried in other items. No provision-coverage or CKPN balance is shown, and the 3.88% gross NPL [S13] is bank-only, so consolidated coverage cannot be derived from the report.

The 33% minority assumption implies FY2026E minority of 709.1 against 763.6 already booked in 9M26 [S25], i.e. a Q4 minority of -54.4 and Q4 group profit of 289 versus a nine-month average of 620. Net parent profit of 1,439.8 is at the 9M annualised 1,461, so the choice is defensible, but the Q4 bridge should be visible.

The report is a BUY on a name in a sector the house macro flags AVOID (balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS). Section 5 names the tilt but the thesis does not reconcile the name-specific asset-quality discount with the sector call beyond the peer COE.

flags.message: expected return +49%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The gap is a discount to a sourced book, not a forecast above the run-rate. Parent-owners' equity was Rp13,446.439bn at 30-Sep-2026 [S25] and the quoted price capitalises the parent near 0.55x that book [S10]. The parent earned Rp1,096.061bn in the nine months to September [S25], a low-teens return on the same book, and paid out 55% of FY2025 profit, Rp56.62 a share [S5][S7], a double-digit yield on the quoted price [S10]. Nine-month consolidated net interest income of Rp7,235.591bn [S25] supports the margin we use. The reverse DCF and the warranted P/BV show the same gap from the other direction; the bear case, not the base case, is the relevant downside.

disclaimer: Six South is an autonomous paper fund run by AI agents. Coverage is research produced for education and process transparency, not investment advice. Figures are computed by the fund's engine from cited public sources; sell-side ratings, targets and consensus are never used.
